variants.name: Pure mapping functions / dataclass pairs
variants.idiom_name: explicit mapping function over dict/dataclass pairs (json module for the wire layer)
variants.implementation_notes: The local idiom is a pure function mapping one plain shape to another (dict in, dict out) or a @dataclass pair with asdict/replace doing the mechanical part; json.loads/json.dumps own the wire layer, with object_hook/default as the hooks when a custom type must decode or encode (docs.python.org json). The classic Translator class adds nothing unless the mapping needs injected collaborators, so keep the function pure and total; when the seam receives untrusted payloads, pydantic models turn the same mapping into declarative validation with field aliases and field_validators and emit the target with model_dump(by_alias=True, mode="json").
pitfalls: json.loads produces arbitrarily large ints and binary floats: a money field translated through a float loses cents, so use Decimal/int minor units at the boundary.
Mutating the incoming dict in place (msg["id"] = msg.pop("order_id")) makes the translator non-idempotent and breaks redelivery, because the second pass sees the already-translated shape.
datetime, Decimal and Enum are not JSON-serialisable: json.dumps raises TypeError at the seam, and default=str quietly changes the representation downstream instead of failing.

variants.name: Pydantic models with aliases and validators
variants.implementation_notes: Declare one model per side of the seam and let pydantic do both halves: Field(alias="order_id") maps the wire name, field_validator/AfterValidator normalise values, and model_dump(by_alias=True, mode="json") emits the target shape with JSON-compatible types only (pydantic serialization concepts). Choose it when the boundary receives untrusted or schema-less payloads and you want the validation and translation to be one declaration; the cost is a dependency and validation errors expressed as exception trees rather than return codes.
pitfalls: ValidationError is raised on the whole document, so a single bad field rejects the message; catch it at the consumer and map it to the invalid-message path instead of letting it propagate.
model_dump() without mode="json" returns non-JSON types (datetime, Decimal) that json.dumps then refuses, and by_alias defaults to False - forgetting it emits the Python field names.

Field validators run only through validation; assigning to an already-built model bypasses them unless validate_assignment is enabled, so a translation that constructs then mutates skips its own rules.
